headings.text: 3 Negative of a vector and multiplication by a scalar

html:
The big picture

Some quantities are fully given by a number and a unit (scalars: mass, time); others also have a direction (vectors: displacement, velocity, force). A vector is drawn as an arrow and added tip to tail; a minus sign reverses it, and a scalar stretches it. In 3D a vector is a column of three components, so all of this becomes component-by-component arithmetic, and the magnitude follows from Pythagoras. The unit vectors \vec e_x, \vec e_y, \vec e_z (also \vec i, \vec j, \vec k) write a vector as a sum, and any vector splits into magnitude × a unit vector giving its direction. There are two ways to multiply two vectors. The scalar product \vec a \cdot \vec b is a number that measures how much the two point the same way; it is zero exactly when they are orthogonal. The vector product (cross product) \vec a \times \vec b is a vector perpendicular to both, whose length is the area of the parallelogram they span.

1 Scalars and vectors

Lecture: board p. 1 · Giancoli §3-1

A quantity that is fully described by a number and a unit is a scalar: mass, time, temperature, energy. A quantity that also has a direction is a vector: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force. "The car drives at 15 m/s" is a speed (scalar); "15 m/s towards north-east" is a velocity (vector).

A vector is drawn as an arrow: it points in the vector's direction, and its length is proportional to the vector's size. In writing, a vector gets an arrow on top, \vec a, so it can't be confused with a number. The size of a vector is its magnitude, written \lvert\vec a\rvert or, shorter, just a without the arrow: the board writes the lone "a" directly under the magnitude formula (section 4). So v = \lvert\vec v\rvert is a speed and F = \lvert\vec F\rvert the size of a force. A magnitude is never negative.

Where an arrow starts does not matter; only its length and direction do. Two arrows with the same length and direction are the same vector, wherever they are drawn.

Intuition

Think of a vector as an instruction: "go this far in this direction". That is why velocity and force can be vectors: they have a size and a direction, but no fixed place. A position vector is the instruction that takes you from the origin to the point.

Connection

Vectors as ordered lists, the tip-to-tail rule and the norm were the topic of 2.1 Linear Algebra Fundamentals. The notation differs: the Math prep course wrote vectors bold (\mathbf{v}) with components v_1, v_2; physics writes an arrow (\vec{a}) and labels components by axis (a_x, a_y, a_z). Same objects.

2 Adding vectors: tip to tail

Lecture: board p. 1 (middle sketch) · Giancoli §3-2

Vectors have a direction, so they can't simply be added as numbers. A walk of 3 m east followed by 4 m north does not take you 7 m from the start, but 5 m. The rule is tip to tail: draw \vec b starting at the tip of \vec a; the sum \vec c = \vec a + \vec b is the arrow from the start of \vec a to the tip of \vec b.

Board sketch (p. 1, middle): \vec a along the bottom, \vec b starting at the tip of \vec a, and \vec c from the start of \vec a to the tip of \vec b, closing the triangle.

The order does not matter, \vec a + \vec b = \vec b + \vec a: going along \vec b first and then \vec a walks round the other side of a parallelogram and arrives at the same point. Drawing both vectors from the same point and taking the diagonal of the parallelogram (the parallelogram method) gives the same sum. With more than two vectors, keep attaching tip to tail; the sum runs from the first tail to the last tip.

Common mistake — adding lengths instead of vectors

Tempting: \lvert \vec a + \vec b \rvert = \lvert\vec a\rvert + \lvert\vec b\rvert. Only true if both point in exactly the same direction. Two forces of 3 N and 4 N at right angles give a resultant of \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5 N, not 7 N; pulling in opposite directions gives 1 N. Vectors of 20 and 40 units can add up to anything from 20 to 60 units, depending on the angle. Always add the components (section 4) first, then take the length.

3 Negative of a vector and multiplication by a scalar

Lecture: board p. 1 · Giancoli §3-3

The negative of a vector, -\vec a, has the same length as \vec a but points the opposite way. The board's bottom sketch on p. 1 shows exactly this: two arrows of equal length, \vec a to the right and \vec b to the left. They have equal magnitude but are not equal vectors: \lvert\vec a\rvert = \lvert\vec b\rvert, but \vec b = -\vec a. The minus sign says something about the direction, never about the length. Subtracting a vector means adding its negative: \vec a - \vec b = \vec a + (-\vec b).

Product with a scalar. Multiplying a vector by a number k multiplies every component by k (board p. 1):

k \cdot \vec{a} = \begin{pmatrix} k \cdot a_x \\ k \cdot a_y \\ k \cdot a_z \end{pmatrix}
Symbols
  • k — a scalar: an ordinary number, possibly with a unit (a mass, a time)
  • \vec{a} — the vector being scaled; a_x, a_y, a_z its components (section 4)
  • k \cdot \vec{a} — the scaled vector

Board sketch: \vec a (blue) and, continuing on the same line, a longer green arrow k\vec a.

Every component is multiplied by the same k, so the ratios between the components, which fix the direction, stay the same: the arrow stays on its line. Its length becomes \lvert k\rvert times as long. With the magnitude formula from section 4:

\lvert k\vec a\rvert = \sqrt{(k a_x)^2 + (k a_y)^2 + (k a_z)^2} = \sqrt{k^2\,(a_x^2 + a_y^2 + a_z^2)} = \lvert k\rvert\,\lvert\vec a\rvert
Symbols
  • symbols as above; \sqrt{k^2} = \lvert k\rvert, the size of k without its sign

For k > 1 the arrow gets longer (the sketch), for 0 < k < 1 shorter, and a negative k also flips it. k = -1 gives the negative of the vector. If k has a unit, the product is a new kind of quantity: in \vec{F} = m\,\vec{a} the force is the acceleration times the scalar m > 0, so force and acceleration always point the same way.

4 Components and magnitude

Lecture: board p. 1, p. 3 (magnitude repeated) · Giancoli §3-4

Drawing and measuring arrows is slow and inaccurate, and impossible in 3D. The precise method uses components. Choose a right-handed x, y, z coordinate system. Any vector can then be written as the column of how far it reaches along each axis:

\vec{a} = \begin{pmatrix} a_x \\ a_y \\ a_z \end{pmatrix}
Symbols
  • \vec{a} — a vector
  • a_x, a_y, a_z — its components: how far the arrow reaches along the x-, y- and z-axis; same unit as the vector (m for a position); negative if it points along the negative axis

The red dashed lines in the top sketch are the "shadows" of the tip of \vec a on the three axes: walk a_x along x, then a_y along y, then a_z up, and you arrive at the tip. That is all a column of components means. The blue curve through the tip is most likely a path along which the point moves, a preview of 4 Kinematics – Position, Velocity and Acceleration, where \vec a becomes a position that changes with time.

Adding by components. The tip-to-tail rule turns into adding the columns entry by entry:

\vec{c} = \vec{a} + \vec{b} = \begin{pmatrix} a_x + b_x \\ a_y + b_y \\ a_z + b_z \end{pmatrix}
Symbols
  • \vec{a}, \vec{b} — the two vectors being added (same physical unit, e.g. both forces in N)
  • a_x, b_x, etc. — their components along each axis
  • \vec{c} — the resultant (sum) vector

Why: walking along \vec a moves you a_x in x, walking on along \vec b a further b_x, so the total in x is a_x + b_x. The axes don't interfere with each other, so the same happens independently in y and z. Subtraction and scalar multiples work the same way, entry by entry.

Magnitude. The length of a vector follows from its components:

\lvert \vec{a} \rvert = \sqrt{a_x^2 + a_y^2 + a_z^2}
Symbols
  • \lvert \vec{a} \rvert — magnitude (length) of \vec{a}, also written a; always \ge 0, same unit as the components
  • a_x, a_y, a_z — components of \vec{a}

It comes from Pythagoras, used twice on the top sketch:

\begin{aligned} d^2 &= a_x^2 + a_y^2 && \text{(right triangle on the floor: legs } a_x, a_y\text{, hypotenuse } d) \\ \lvert\vec a\rvert^2 &= d^2 + a_z^2 && \text{(right triangle standing up: legs } d, a_z\text{, hypotenuse } \lvert\vec a\rvert) \\ &= a_x^2 + a_y^2 + a_z^2 && \text{(insert the first line)} \\ \lvert\vec a\rvert &= \sqrt{a_x^2 + a_y^2 + a_z^2} && \text{(positive root: a length is} \ge 0) \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • d — length of the "floor diagonal", the shadow of \vec a in the x–y plane (an auxiliary length, not on the board)
  • a_x, a_y, a_z, \lvert\vec a\rvert — as above

The second triangle has a right angle because a_z stands vertically on the floor. Squaring also makes the signs of the components irrelevant: (-3)^2 = 3^2. A consequence: no component can be longer than the vector itself.

Beyond the lecture (Giancoli §3-4)

In a plane, a vector can be given either by its components or by its magnitude V and the angle \theta it makes with the positive x-axis (counted anticlockwise). From the right triangle formed by the vector and its components: V_x = V\cos\theta, V_y = V\sin\theta, and back: V = \sqrt{V_x^2 + V_y^2}, \tan\theta = V_y/V_x (check the quadrant from the signs). The lecture uses exactly this in 6 Projectile Motion (v_{0x} = v_0\cos\alpha) and on inclines in 9 Free-Body Diagrams and Friction.

Worked example — adding, scaling and measuring vectors

Positions \vec a = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{m} and \vec b = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{m}.

  1. Add component by component: \vec c = \vec a + \vec b = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{m}.
  2. Length of \vec a (Pythagoras in 3D): \lvert\vec a\rvert = \sqrt{2^2 + (-1)^2 + 2^2}\,\mathrm{m} = \sqrt{9}\,\mathrm{m} = 3\,\mathrm{m}.
  3. Length of the sum: \lvert\vec c\rvert = \sqrt{9 + 4 + 0}\,\mathrm{m} = \sqrt{13}\,\mathrm{m} \approx 3.61\,\mathrm{m}, while \lvert\vec a\rvert + \lvert\vec b\rvert = 3\,\mathrm{m} + \sqrt{14}\,\mathrm{m} \approx 6.74\,\mathrm{m}. Lengths don't add.
  4. Scale by a negative number: -2\,\vec a = \begin{pmatrix} -4 \\ 2 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{m}, twice as long (6\,\mathrm{m}) and pointing the opposite way.
Problem-solving steps — adding vectors by components
  1. Draw the vectors tip to tail, so you know roughly what the sum should look like.
  2. Choose the axes; if possible, put one axis along one of the vectors so it has only one component.
  3. Write every vector as a column of components (from an angle: V\cos\theta, V\sin\theta), with a minus sign for every component along a negative axis.
  4. Add the x-components, the y-components and the z-components separately.
  5. If magnitude and direction are asked: \lvert\vec c\rvert = \sqrt{c_x^2 + c_y^2 + c_z^2}; check that the signs fit the sketch.

5 Unit vectors: magnitude and direction

Lecture: board p. 1 (unit vectors), p. 3 ("F = 100\ \mathrm N" block) · Giancoli §3-5

A unit vector is a vector of length exactly 1, used only to point in a direction. The three along the axes are:

\vec{e}_x = \vec{i} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \vec{e}_y = \vec{j} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \vec{e}_z = \vec{k} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}
Symbols
  • \vec{e}_x, \vec{e}_y, \vec{e}_z — the unit vectors along the three axes: length 1, dimensionless, pointing in the positive x, y, z direction (the small green arrows in the top sketch)
  • \vec{i}, \vec{j}, \vec{k} — common alternative names for the same three vectors

With them, any vector can be written as a sum (board p. 1):

\vec{a} = a_x \cdot \vec{e}_x + a_y \cdot \vec{e}_y + a_z \cdot \vec{e}_z = a_x \cdot \vec{i} + a_y \cdot \vec{j} + a_z \cdot \vec{k}
Symbols
  • a_x, a_y, a_z — components of \vec{a} (they carry the unit, e.g. m)
  • \vec{e}_x, \ldots and \vec i, \ldots — the unit vectors as above

This is the same as the column, by the two rules from section 3 and 4 (scale, then add):

a_x\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + a_y\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + a_z\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a_x \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ a_y \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ a_z \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a_x \\ a_y \\ a_z \end{pmatrix}

Symbols as above. The sum form is handy inline: \vec{F} = (3\,\vec i - 2\,\vec k)\,\mathrm{N} means F_x = 3\,\mathrm{N}, F_y = 0, F_z = -2\,\mathrm{N}.

Magnitude × direction. On p. 3 the board makes one idea explicit: any vector splits into "how much" times "which way", where "which way" is a unit vector:

\boxed{F = 100\ \mathrm N} \qquad \vec F = \underbrace{100}_{\text{magn.}} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{\text{direction } \vec d}\ \mathrm{N}, \qquad \lvert\vec d\rvert = 1
\vec F = \begin{pmatrix} F_x \\ F_y \\ F_z \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 100\ \mathrm{N} \\ 0\ \mathrm{N} \\ 0\ \mathrm{N} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 100 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\mathrm{N}
Symbols
  • F — magnitude of the force (N), a scalar ("magn." on the board); \vec F — the force vector
  • \vec d — the direction of the force as a unit vector (length 1, dimensionless); here the x-direction \vec e_x
  • F_x, F_y, F_z — components of \vec F (N)

The last two columns show that the unit can be written once outside the column: it is the same for every component, so it factors out like any common factor. In general:

\vec F = F \cdot \vec d, \quad \lvert\vec d\rvert = 1 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \vec d = \frac{\vec F}{\lvert\vec F\rvert} \quad (\vec F \neq \vec 0)

Symbols as above. The second form is how you get the direction of a given vector: divide it by its length. Example: \vec F = (3, 0, -4)^\top\,\mathrm{N} has F = 5\,\mathrm{N}, so \vec d = (0.6,\ 0,\ -0.8)^\top, and indeed 0.6^2 + 0.8^2 = 1. The zero vector has no direction, which is why \vec F \neq \vec 0 is needed.

6 Scalar product ("dot product")

Lecture: board p. 2 (from "09.10.2026") – p. 3 top · Giancoli §7-2

Multiplying a vector by a scalar (section 3) stretches it. Multiplying two vectors with each other can be defined in two useful ways: one gives a number, the other a vector (section 7). The first is needed for work: only the part of a force that points along the motion does work (11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy › 5 Work done by a constant force), so we need "how much of \vec b lies along \vec a".

Definition from the angle. Draw both vectors from the same point; let \varphi be the angle between them. Then

\vec a \cdot \vec b = \lvert\vec a\rvert \cdot \lvert\vec b\rvert \cdot \cos\varphi
Symbols
  • \vec a \cdot \vec b — the scalar product: a number (scalar), not a vector; its unit is the product of the two units (e.g. N·m)
  • \lvert\vec a\rvert, \lvert\vec b\rvert — the magnitudes of the two vectors, \ge 0
  • \varphi — the angle between the two vectors drawn from the same point (tails together), 0^\circ \le \varphi \le 180^\circ

Board sketch: \vec b drawn from the same point as \vec a, at the angle \varphi to it.

Unclear (p. 2): absolute-value bars on the left

The board writes \lvert \vec a \cdot \vec b \rvert = \lvert\vec a\rvert\,\lvert\vec b\rvert\cos\varphi. The scalar product itself has no bars: for 90^\circ < \varphi \le 180^\circ the cosine is negative, so \vec a \cdot \vec b is negative, which an absolute value can't be. The component formula below gives the same signed number. Use the version without bars.

Meaning: magnitude times projection. \lvert\vec b\rvert\cos\varphi is the component (projection) of \vec b along the direction of \vec a: how far \vec b reaches along \vec a. The scalar product is that projection times \lvert\vec a\rvert (or, equally, the projection of \vec a on \vec b times \lvert\vec b\rvert). This is exactly the form of work: W = \vec F\cdot\Delta\vec r = F\,\Delta r\cos\varphi.

Intuition

Shine a light perpendicular onto the line of \vec a: \lvert\vec b\rvert\cos\varphi is the length of \vec b's shadow on that line, negative if the shadow falls backwards. The scalar product is "\lvert\vec a\rvert times \vec b's shadow".

The special angles. The board writes \cos 0^\circ = 1 and \cos 90^\circ = 0 next to a second sketch with \vec b at a right angle to \vec a, and concludes \vec a \cdot \vec b = 0:

  • \varphi = 0^\circ (same direction): \vec a \cdot \vec b = \lvert\vec a\rvert\lvert\vec b\rvert, the largest possible value.
  • \varphi = 90^\circ: \vec a \cdot \vec b = 0. Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular (orthogonal) exactly when their scalar product is 0. (A zero scalar product can also mean that one of the vectors is \vec 0.)
  • Between 90^\circ and 180^\circ the scalar product is negative: the vectors point "against" each other; at 180^\circ it is -\lvert\vec a\rvert\lvert\vec b\rvert.

Order doesn't matter. \lvert\vec a\rvert, \lvert\vec b\rvert and \cos\varphi are numbers, so \vec a\cdot\vec b = \vec b\cdot\vec a (commutative).

Beyond the lecture (Giancoli §7-2)

The scalar product is also distributive: \vec a\cdot(\vec b + \vec c) = \vec a\cdot\vec b + \vec a\cdot\vec c (the projections of \vec b and \vec c along \vec a add up to the projection of their sum). This rule is what turns the angle definition into the component formula below.

From the components. Write both vectors with the unit vectors of section 5, \vec a = a_x\vec e_x + a_y\vec e_y + a_z\vec e_z and \vec b = b_x\vec e_x + b_y\vec e_y + b_z\vec e_z. The unit vectors have length 1 and are perpendicular to each other, so by the angle definition

\vec e_x\cdot\vec e_x = \vec e_y\cdot\vec e_y = \vec e_z\cdot\vec e_z = 1, \qquad \vec e_x\cdot\vec e_y = \vec e_x\cdot\vec e_z = \vec e_y\cdot\vec e_z = 0
Symbols
  • \vec e_x, \vec e_y, \vec e_z (also \vec i, \vec j, \vec k) — the unit vectors along the axes, length 1, mutually perpendicular

Multiplying out (a_x\vec e_x + a_y\vec e_y + a_z\vec e_z)\cdot(b_x\vec e_x + b_y\vec e_y + b_z\vec e_z) term by term gives nine products; the six with two different unit vectors are 0, the three with equal ones carry a factor 1. What remains is the formula on the board, which needs no angle:

\vec a \cdot \vec b = a_x \cdot b_x + a_y \cdot b_y + a_z \cdot b_z \quad \text{(a SCALAR)}
Symbols
  • a_x, a_y, a_z and b_x, b_y, b_z — the components of \vec a and \vec b
  • the result is one number: multiply matching components, then add
Why do the two formulas give the same number? (a second route, without the distributive law)

Compute the third side of the triangle formed by \vec a, \vec b and \vec a - \vec b in two ways. Law of cosines: \lvert\vec a - \vec b\rvert^2 = \lvert\vec a\rvert^2 + \lvert\vec b\rvert^2 - 2\lvert\vec a\rvert\lvert\vec b\rvert\cos\varphi. Magnitude formula on \vec a - \vec b: \lvert\vec a - \vec b\rvert^2 = (a_x - b_x)^2 + (a_y - b_y)^2 + (a_z - b_z)^2 = \lvert\vec a\rvert^2 + \lvert\vec b\rvert^2 - 2\,(a_x b_x + a_y b_y + a_z b_z) (binomial formula three times, then regroup the squares). Both describe the same length, so a_x b_x + a_y b_y + a_z b_z = \lvert\vec a\rvert\lvert\vec b\rvert\cos\varphi.

The board's examples.

\vec a = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \vec b = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}: \qquad \vec a \cdot \vec b = \underbrace{1 \cdot 2}_{x} + \underbrace{0 \cdot 0}_{y} + \underbrace{1 \cdot 2}_{z} = 4

Symbols as above. Here \vec b = 2\vec a, so the two point the same way and \varphi should be 0^\circ. Check: \lvert\vec a\rvert = \sqrt2, \lvert\vec b\rvert = 2\sqrt2, so \cos\varphi = 4/(\sqrt2 \cdot 2\sqrt2) = 1 ✓.

\vec a = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \vec b = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}: \qquad \vec a \cdot \vec b = 1 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 0 = 0

Symbols as above. These are \vec e_x and \vec e_y: the axes are perpendicular, so the "\cos 90^\circ = 0" case appears in numbers. This is one of the six zero products used in the derivation above.

Magnitude as a scalar product. The board then repeats \lvert\vec a\rvert = \sqrt{a_x^2 + a_y^2 + a_z^2} (top of p. 3). It is a scalar product: take \vec b = \vec a, so \varphi = 0^\circ:

\vec a \cdot \vec a = a_x^2 + a_y^2 + a_z^2 = \lvert\vec a\rvert\,\lvert\vec a\rvert\cos 0^\circ = \lvert\vec a\rvert^2 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \lvert\vec a\rvert = \sqrt{\vec a \cdot \vec a}

Symbols as above.

The angle between two vectors. With both formulas in hand, solving the angle form for \cos\varphi gives the standard use of the scalar product:

\cos\varphi = \frac{\vec a \cdot \vec b}{\lvert\vec a\rvert\,\lvert\vec b\rvert} \qquad (\vec a, \vec b \neq \vec 0)

Symbols as above.

Worked example — the angle between two vectors

\vec a = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}, \vec b = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}.

  1. Scalar product from components: \vec a \cdot \vec b = 3 \cdot 4 + 0 \cdot 0 + 4 \cdot 3 = 24.
  2. Magnitudes: \lvert\vec a\rvert = \sqrt{9 + 0 + 16} = 5, \lvert\vec b\rvert = 5.
  3. Cosine: \cos\varphi = \dfrac{24}{5 \cdot 5} = 0.96.
  4. Angle: \varphi = \arccos(0.96) \approx 16.3^\circ.
  5. Check: positive scalar product → angle below 90^\circ ✓; the vectors are nearly parallel ✓.
Worked example — work as a scalar product

A force \vec F = (20,\ 10,\ 0)^\top\ \mathrm N acts on a body that moves by \Delta\vec r = (3,\ -2,\ 0)^\top\ \mathrm m.

  1. Components: W = \vec F\cdot\Delta\vec r = 20\cdot3 + 10\cdot(-2) + 0\cdot0 = 40\ \mathrm J.
  2. Meaning: the y part of the force points against the y part of the motion and takes 20 J off the 60 J of the x part.
  3. Check with the angle: \lvert\vec F\rvert = 22.4\ \mathrm N, \lvert\Delta\vec r\rvert = 3.61\ \mathrm m, \cos\varphi = 40/(22.4\cdot3.61) = 0.496, \varphi = 60.3^\circ; 22.4\cdot3.61\cdot0.496 = 40\ \mathrm J ✓.
Common mistake — a scalar product that comes out as a vector

Tempting: \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}, multiplying component by component and stopping. That forgets the sum: the scalar product is the single number 2 + 0 + 2 = 4. If your answer to "\vec a \cdot \vec b" is a column, something is wrong.

Problem-solving steps — angle between two vectors, or testing for a right angle
  1. Compute \vec a \cdot \vec b from the components (multiply matching entries, add).
  2. To test for perpendicularity, stop here: 0 means perpendicular (for non-zero vectors).
  3. Otherwise compute both magnitudes.
  4. \cos\varphi = \vec a \cdot \vec b / (\lvert\vec a\rvert\lvert\vec b\rvert), then \varphi = \arccos(\ldots).
  5. Check the sign: positive → acute angle, negative → obtuse angle.
Connection

The math prep course introduced the dot product with the same two formulas: 2.1 Linear Algebra Fundamentals › Dot product and angle. In mechanics it gives the work W = \vec F\cdot\Delta\vec r and the power P = \vec F\cdot\vec v (11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy).

7 Vector product ("cross product")

Lecture: board p. 3 – p. 4 top · Giancoli §11-2

The second product of two vectors gives a vector. The board: CROSS PRODUCT → VECTOR PRODUCT, \vec a \times \vec b. It is needed wherever a turning effect matters, such as torque.

Definition: magnitude and direction. \vec a \times \vec b is the vector whose magnitude is

\lvert \vec a \times \vec b \rvert = \lvert\vec a\rvert \cdot \lvert\vec b\rvert \cdot \sin\varphi = A
Symbols
  • \vec a \times \vec b — the vector product, a vector (in the sketch called \vec c)
  • A = \lvert\vec a \times \vec b\rvert — its magnitude, equal to the area of the parallelogram spanned by \vec a and \vec b (unit: the product of the two units, e.g. m² for two lengths)
  • \varphi — the angle between \vec a and \vec b, tails together (0^\circ \le \varphi \le 180^\circ)

and whose direction is perpendicular to both \vec a and \vec b, in the sense of the right-hand rule: fingers along \vec a, curl them towards \vec b through the smaller angle, and the thumb shows \vec a \times \vec b.

The magnitude is the parallelogram's area (the board's A). Take \vec a as the base. The height is the distance from the tip of \vec b straight down to the line of \vec a (the dashed line with the right-angle mark). In the right triangle formed by \vec b, that height and the base line, \vec b is the hypotenuse and the height lies opposite \varphi:

\text{height} = \lvert\vec b\rvert\sin\varphi \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad A = \text{base} \cdot \text{height} = \lvert\vec a\rvert \cdot \lvert\vec b\rvert\sin\varphi

Symbols as above; \sin\varphi = \text{opposite}/\text{hypotenuse}. Parallel vectors (\varphi = 0^\circ or 180^\circ) span no area, so their cross product is the zero vector; perpendicular ones give the maximum, \lvert\vec a\rvert\lvert\vec b\rvert.

The direction on the board. The sketch draws \vec c standing upright on the parallelogram, with the axes beside it: turning from x to y, the right-hand rule gives z, so \vec e_x \times \vec e_y = \vec e_z.

Intuition

The scalar product asks "how much do they point the same way?" (cosine); the vector product asks "how much do they point across each other?" (sine), and answers with an arrow standing on the plane they span.

From the components. The board shows the columns of \vec a and \vec b side by side with coloured crossing lines between them, and the determinant notation as a memory aid:

\vec a \times \vec b = \begin{vmatrix} \vec i & \vec j & \vec k \\ a_x & a_y & a_z \\ b_x & b_y & b_z \end{vmatrix} = \vec c = \begin{pmatrix} a_y \cdot b_z - a_z \cdot b_y \\ a_z \cdot b_x - a_x \cdot b_z \\ a_x \cdot b_y - a_y \cdot b_x \end{pmatrix}
Symbols
  • \vec i, \vec j, \vec k — the unit vectors along x, y, z
  • a_x, \ldots, b_z — components of \vec a and \vec b
  • \lvert \cdots \rvert with three rows — a 3 \times 3 determinant, used here only as a memory aid (its first row holds vectors, not numbers)
  • \vec c — the resulting vector, as a column of its x-, y-, z-components

Reading the crossing lines: for each component, leave out the matching row and cross-multiply the other two, "down-right minus up-right":

  • x-component, from the y and z rows: a_y b_z - a_z b_y (boxed on the board);
  • y-component, from z and x: a_z b_x - a_x b_z;
  • z-component, from x and y: a_x b_y - a_y b_x.

The pattern is cyclic: the x-entry uses y, z; the y-entry uses z, x; the z-entry uses x, y, always "the next one times the one after" (x \to y \to z \to x) minus the reverse. The empty column "= [\ \ldots\ ]" on the board is a placeholder for inserting numbers.

The rule of Sarrus (p. 4 top) evaluates the determinant: the first two columns are written again to the right, and red arrows mark the diagonals:

\begin{matrix} \vec i & \vec j & \vec k & \vec i & \vec j \\ a_x & a_y & a_z & a_x & a_y \\ b_x & b_y & b_z & b_x & b_y \end{matrix}

Symbols as above. The board writes out the six products, circling the \vec i terms red (x), the \vec j terms green (y) and the \vec k terms black (z):

\vec a \times \vec b = \vec i \cdot a_y b_z + \vec j \cdot a_z b_x + \vec k\, a_x b_y - \vec j \cdot a_x b_z - \vec i \cdot a_z b_y - \vec k \cdot a_y b_x

Symbols as above. Step by step:

  1. Three diagonals down to the right, each with +: from \vec i: \vec i\,a_y b_z; from \vec j: \vec j\,a_z b_x; from \vec k: \vec k\,a_x b_y.
  2. Three diagonals up to the right (starting in the bottom row), each with -: from b_x: \vec k\,a_y b_x; from b_y: \vec i\,a_z b_y; from b_z: \vec j\,a_x b_z.
  3. Collect by unit vector (that is what the colours do): \vec a \times \vec b = \vec i\,(a_y b_z - a_z b_y) + \vec j\,(a_z b_x - a_x b_z) + \vec k\,(a_x b_y - a_y b_x).
  4. Turn it into a column. That is what the board's last line "\Rightarrow \vec i = (1, 0, 0)^\top" means: as in section 5, the bracket in front of \vec i is the x-component, the one in front of \vec j the y-component, the one in front of \vec k the z-component. The result is the column formula above.

Properties that follow. From the definition (or the component formula):

  • \vec a\times\vec a = \vec 0, and more generally parallel vectors give \vec 0 (\sin 0^\circ = 0);
  • \vec b\times\vec a = -\,\vec a\times\vec b: swapping the order turns the right-hand thumb round (each component changes sign);
  • for the unit vectors: \vec e_x\times\vec e_y = \vec e_z, \vec e_y\times\vec e_z = \vec e_x, \vec e_z\times\vec e_x = \vec e_y (cyclic), and \vec e_x\times\vec e_x = \vec 0 etc.
Beyond the lecture (Giancoli §11-2)

The cross product is distributive, \vec a\times(\vec b + \vec c) = \vec a\times\vec b + \vec a\times\vec c, but not commutative (see above) and not associative. The book also uses it to write torque as a vector, \vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F, which 10 Torque, Gravitation, Work and Energy › 5 Torque and equilibrium: the forklift mentions.

Why is \vec a \times \vec b perpendicular to both \vec a and \vec b?

Check with the scalar product: perpendicular means scalar product 0. \vec c \cdot \vec a = (a_y b_z - a_z b_y)\,a_x + (a_z b_x - a_x b_z)\,a_y + (a_x b_y - a_y b_x)\,a_z. Multiply out: every term appears twice with opposite signs (e.g. a_x a_y b_z and -a_x a_y b_z), so the sum is 0. The same happens for \vec c \cdot \vec b. So the component formula really builds a vector standing upright on the parallelogram.

Worked example — cross product and a check of its length

\vec a = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \vec b = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} (both in the x–y plane).

  1. Components: c_x = 2 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 1 = 0; c_y = 0 \cdot 3 - 1 \cdot 0 = 0; c_z = 1 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 3 = -5. So \vec a \times \vec b = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ -5 \end{pmatrix}.
  2. Direction check: both vectors lie in the x–y plane, so the product must point along z ✓. It points to -z: turning from \vec a to \vec b is clockwise seen from above.
  3. Length check with the angle: \cos\varphi = \dfrac{\vec a \cdot \vec b}{\lvert\vec a\rvert\lvert\vec b\rvert} = \dfrac{5}{\sqrt5\,\sqrt{10}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, so \varphi = 45^\circ and \lvert\vec a\rvert\lvert\vec b\rvert\sin\varphi = \sqrt{50} \cdot \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = 5 ✓; the parallelogram has area 5.
Common mistake — swapping the order or a sign

Unlike ordinary multiplication, the order matters: \vec b \times \vec a = -(\vec a \times \vec b). In the example, \vec b \times \vec a = (0, 0, 5)^\top. The other trap is the middle component: it is a_z b_x - a_x b_z, not a_x b_z - a_z b_x. Use the cyclic pattern.

Problem-solving steps — computing a cross product
  1. Write both vectors as columns, \vec a first (the order matters).
  2. Each entry: leave out its own row, cross-multiply the other two in cyclic order (x: a_y b_z - a_z b_y; y: a_z b_x - a_x b_z; z: a_x b_y - a_y b_x), or use Sarrus.
  3. Check perpendicularity: \vec c \cdot \vec a = 0 and \vec c \cdot \vec b = 0.
  4. If needed, the area is \lvert\vec c\rvert; check the direction with the right-hand rule.
